summary: To ask a yes/no question, put 吗 (ma) at the end of the statement: 你要黄瓜。→ 你要黄瓜吗？ Nothing else moves. A second way repeats the verb with 不 in between (A-not-A): 你要不要黄瓜？ — then without 吗; with 有 it is 有没有. There is no all-purpose ‘yes’ or ‘no’: you answer by repeating the verb (要。/ 不要。, 有。/ 没有。, 是。/ 不是。).

blocks.title: Question words never take 吗
blocks.text: 你喝什么？ ‘What do you drink?’ — with 吗 (你喝什么吗？) it means ‘Do you drink anything?’.

askYourself: Is there already a question word (什么, 哪里 …)? → no 吗.
Is it a yes/no question? → statement + 吗, or verb-不-verb.
Did I use verb-不-verb (要不要, 是不是)? → then no 吗.
Is the verb 有? → the A-not-A form is 有没有.
How do I answer? → repeat the verb, or its negation (要 / 不要; 有 / 没有; 是 / 不是).
steps: Write the statement in normal word order.
Add 吗 before the question mark — or replace the verb by verb + 不 + verb.

traps: *你喝什么吗？ for ‘what do you drink?’ — 什么 + 吗 means ‘anything’.
*你要不要黄瓜吗？ — A-not-A and 吗 never combine.
Don’t imitate English inversion or ‘do’: 你要黄瓜吗？ keeps the statement order.
Answering 是 to every question sounds wrong: to 你要黄瓜吗？ answer 要。, not 是。

seeAlso.note: German puts the verb first (Bist du Student?); Chinese keeps the statement order and adds 吗.
Arabic opens the question with hal or ʾa-; Chinese closes it with 吗.
Hebrew often uses intonation alone (or ha-im at the start); Chinese keeps its tones and uses 吗 instead.
